nameStory: Beaked Hawkweed gets its name from the pointed, beak-like tips on its seeds that help them catch the wind and spread to new locations. The 'hawkweed' part comes from an old belief that hawks ate these plants to sharpen their eyesight, though there's no truth to this medieval legend.
description: Beaked Hawkweed is a hairy wildflower that grows up to about 2.5 feet tall from a cluster of leaves at its base. It produces small, bright yellow daisy-like flowers that are only about a third of an inch across - much smaller than most flowers in the sunflower family. The plant has a distinctly fuzzy appearance, especially at the bottom of its stem, and blooms from late spring through fall.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellow flowers only 8mm across with classic daisy shape, appearing in loose clusters at stem tips from May through October

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows from a rosette of basal leaves with hairy stems that are much fuzzier at the bottom than the top

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large spoon-shaped leaves up to 8 inches long cluster at the base, while smaller alternate leaves climb sparsely up the stem

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Feel distinctly hairy and rough to the touch, especially the lower portion which is noticeably fuzzier than the upper stem

habitat: Look for Beaked Hawkweed in dry, rocky areas with open canopy - it thrives in poor soils where other plants struggle. You'll often find it in open woodlands with thin soil, rocky slopes, old fields, and forest edges. It prefers spots with good drainage and partial to full sun.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in rosettes close to the ground, and first flowers may appear by late May in warmer areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with small yellow flowers continuously opening throughout the season on increasingly tall, hairy stems.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering into October, with fluffy seed heads developing that will disperse on autumn winds.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only dried stems that may persist through snow.

funFact: Despite being called 'queendevil' in some regions, this humble plant is actually quite well-behaved and doesn't spread aggressively like some of its more notorious hawkweed cousins that can take over entire meadows.
confusionNotes: The tiny flowers are the key - most other yellow wildflowers in New England have much larger blooms. If you're looking at yellow flowers smaller than a dime on a very hairy plant, you've likely found a hawkweed.
contextualKnowledge: Hawkweeds can be tricky to identify to species level even for experts, as they hybridize freely and have variable characteristics. Don't worry if you can only get to 'hawkweed' - even botanists sometimes struggle with the finer distinctions in this group.
compareHints: Among New England's hawkweeds, Beaked Hawkweed stands out for its extremely small flowers and very hairy lower stem. Panicled Hawkweed has a more branched flower cluster, while Rattlesnakeweed has distinctive purple-veined leaves. The tiny flower size is really your best clue for Beaked Hawkweed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Panicled hawkweed stands out from its hawkweed relatives by being much taller and more upright than species like rattlesnakeweed or spotted hawkweed.
Among its hawkweed relatives, rattlesnakeweed stands out for its ground-hugging rosette growth pattern and prominent leaf veining.
Rough hawkweed is much more bristly and hairy than its relatives like panicled hawkweed or Canada hawkweed, which have smoother stems and leaves.
Among the many hawkweed species in New England, common hawkweed is distinguished by its branching growth habit and grayish, hairy leaves.
Among New England's hawkweeds, this species stands out for its multi-branched flowering stems and medium height.
Among New England hawkweeds, Canada hawkweed stands out for its exceptionally narrow, smooth leaves and tall, elegant stature.
Among New England's hawkweeds, spotted hawkweed stands out for its tall, branching flower stems and tendency to grow in disturbed soils.
Among New England's hawkweeds, wall hawkweed is distinguished by its preference for rocky, vertical surfaces and its distinctly heart-shaped leaves with purple veining.
Among its hawkweed relatives, Robinson's hawkweed stays much smaller than New England hawkweed or Canada hawkweed, which can grow much taller.
